area: Quantitative realism benchmarking for (a) microscopic traffic simulation and (b) V2X communication simulation — metrics, numeric thresholds, reference measurement campaigns, and public calibration datasets (classics + 2024-2026)
benchmarks: GEH statistic: GEH = sqrt(2(m-c)^2/(m+c)) per link/detector. Acceptance (FHWA Traffic Analysis Toolbox Vol III, Wisconsin DOT criteria, UK DMRB/TAG lineage): GEH < 5 for >= 85% of individual link flows; GEH < 4 for the sum of all link flows; GEH < 3 often used as a stricter calibration (not just validation) target.

Link flow tolerances (same FHWA Table): within 15% for 700 < q < 2700 veh/h; within 100 veh/h for q < 700; within 400 veh/h for q > 2700 — each for > 85% of cases; sum of all link flows within 5% of counts.
Travel/journey times: within 15% (or 1 minute, whichever is higher) for >= 85% of routes (FHWA 2004/Wisconsin).

FHWA 2019 update (FHWA-HOP-18-036) distribution-based criteria: (I) 95% of simulated time-series points within the field-data 2-sigma band; (II) 66% within the 1-sigma band (plus 2 non-adjacent critical intervals inside the time-variant envelope); (III) Bounded Dynamic Absolute Error; (IV) Bounded Dynamic Systematic Error.

Car-following calibration on trajectories: spacing/gap RMSPE (root mean square percentage error) — literature state of the art is ~10-30% (inter-driver variability floor per Treiber & Kesting; Punzo et al. calibration guidelines); IDM calibrated per-pair on highD achieves 5.2-6.9% mean gap error (Kurtc 2020, TRR 10.1177/0361198120925063).

Physical plausibility gate on trajectories: acceleration magnitudes must stay in human ranges (~ -8 to +4 m/s^2 hard bound, mostly within +/-3 m/s^2); raw NGSIM violated this massively (noise-driven accelerations of order 10 ft/s^2 and worse), which is the canonical realism failure (Punzo/Montanino & Coifman-Li critiques).

Fundamental diagram anchors for freeway realism: lane capacity ~1800-2400 veh/h/lane; queue-discharge capacity drop ~5-15% (Cassidy & Bertini 1999 and follow-ups); congested/backward wave speed ~15-20 km/h; simulated flow-density scatter should reproduce these three quantities, not just the free-flow branch.

Distributional tests: Kolmogorov-Smirnov (or Anderson-Darling) test on time-headway and saturation-headway distributions vs loop-event or trajectory data (used e.g. to validate SUMO, MDPI su18147025); Wasserstein (earth-mover) distance on speed/headway/trajectory feature distributions — a 2024 pNEUMA-based SUMO calibration reduced Wasserstein distance ~55.8% vs default SUMO parameters, illustrating it as an iterative objective.

Trajectory-level distributional realism (modern): WOSAC 'realism meta-metric' — approximate negative log-likelihood of held-out real trajectories under the simulator's rollout distribution, aggregated over kinematic (speed/accel), interactive (nearest-object distance, collision, TTC) and map-based (road-edge offset, offroad) components over 32 rollouts per scenario.

Platoon dispersion (signalized corridors): downstream arrival-profile spread vs Robertson's TRANSYT model with field-calibrated dispersion factor (classic alpha ~0.35, beta ~0.8) — compare simulated platoon profiles to Robertson-predicted/measured profiles.

V2X PDR-vs-distance reference points: IEEE 802.11p/DSRC LoS open-road — high PDR sustained up to ~500-700 m at ~20 dBm (GM campaigns, Bai-Stancil-Krishnan MobiCom 2010; Sensors 2021 benchmark PMC8347901); urban NLoS collapses to an effective range on the order of only ~100 m at obstructed intersections; a pronounced stochastic 'gray zone' (PDR between ~90% and ~20%) must exist between the reliable zone and cutoff — a step-function range model fails this test.

C-V2X Mode 4: simulation benchmark PDR >= 95% out to 380/300/280 m at densities 0.1/0.2/0.3 veh/m (MCS 9, keep-prob 0.8; Springer 978-3-031-21967-2_45); DLR field test (ITS World Congress 2021): C-V2X PER ~0% (1-sigma) at 200 B rising to 10%/13% at 800/1000 B, and it loses connectivity earlier than ITS-G5 in NLoS.

Latency CDF anchors (DLR Cohda MK5/MK6c field measurements): ITS-G5/802.11p minimum end-to-end latency ~5 ms at 200 B, rising to 8-9 ms at 800/1000 B; C-V2X (LTE PC5 mode 4, SPS) ~25 ms typical, rising to 40-45 ms (1-sigma) for 800-1000 B packets.

Channel load: CBR (fraction of time channel sensed busy, 1 s window) — ETSI DCC satisfactory operating range 0.55-0.75, algorithms hold ~0.6; a comm model at high vehicle density that never approaches these CBR levels (or lacks CBR entirely) cannot reproduce congestion effects on PDR/latency.

Awareness metrics: neighbor awareness ratio = detected neighbors / neighbors physically present within a nominal range, within a freshness window (EURECOM 'Rethinking Cooperative Awareness'); minimum Awareness Failure Distance (mAFD) as the safety-oriented variant (MDPI s24186086). Track NAR at 100/200/300 m vs density.

VeReMi-family dataset-credibility criteria (from its own critique lineage): benign kinematics must carry a sensor/GPS error model (original VeReMi's error-free positions made position attacks nearly linearly separable — fixed in VeReMi Extension); diverse attack families (5 -> 19 -> 15 curated in NextGen); predefined train/val/test splits; modern calibrated traffic scenario (LuST -> InTAS) and documented generator for reproducibility.
findings:
== A. MICROSCOPIC TRAFFIC: metrics, thresholds, standards ==

1) GEH + flow/travel-time criteria (the de-facto industry gate). FHWA Traffic Analysis Toolbox Volume III (2004; Wisconsin DOT freeway criteria, UK DMRB lineage) — verbatim thresholds (https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/trafficanalysistools/tat_vol3/sect5.htm): individual link flows within 15% for 700<q<2700 veh/h, within 100 veh/h for q<700, within 400 veh/h for q>2700, each for >85% of cases; sum of all link flows within 5%; GEH<5 for individual links in >85% of cases; GEH<4 for sum of links; journey times within 15% (or 1 min if higher) for >85%; visually acceptable speed-flow curves and bottleneck queuing. TxDOT's manual (https://www.txdot.gov/manuals/des/tsp/chapter-13-microsimulation-analysis/13-5-calibration.html) restates these and adds that agencies often use GEH<=3 as the calibration (vs validation) target. The FHWA 2019 update (FHWA-HOP-18-036, https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/fhwahop18036/index.htm; summarized at https://www.txdot.gov/manuals/des/tsp/chapter-13-microsimulation-analysis/13-5-calibration/13-5-2-acceptability-criteria/13-5-2-4-fhwa-traffic-analysis-toolbox--volume-iii.html) replaces single-number matching with distribution-based criteria against multi-day field 'variation envelopes': (I) 95% of simulated points inside the 2-sigma band; (II) 66% inside the 1-sigma band + critical-interval condition; (III) Bounded Dynamic Absolute Error; (IV) Bounded Dynamic Systematic Error. Implication for iterative benchmarking: represent the reference as a distribution over days/seeds, not one number.

2) Car-following (trajectory-level) calibration. Standard protocol: per-leader-follower-pair optimization of model params (IDM, Krauss, Gipps, W99) minimizing RMSPE on spacing (preferred over speed — Punzo et al. calibration guidelines; 'Identifiability of car-following dynamics' https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.08652). Anchors: Kurtc (TRR 2020, https://doi.org/10.1177/0361198120925063) calibrated IDM/OVM on highD — mean gap errors 5.2-6.9%; Treiber & Kesting's long-standing result that calibration errors of 10-30% represent the irreducible inter/intra-driver variability floor, so chasing <5% is overfitting. Bayesian variants: 'Bayesian Calibration of the Intelligent Driver Model' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03571), 'Calibrating Car-Following Models via Bayesian Dynamic Regression' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.03340) — both use highD/NGSIM and report posterior predictive checks, useful if you want uncertainty-aware realism scores.

3) Data-quality lesson (NGSIM): raw NGSIM I-80/US-101 trajectories contain physically impossible kinematics — Punzo, Borzacchiello & Ciuffo (TR-C 2011, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0968090X10001701) and Coifman & Li's critical evaluation (TR-B 2017, https://ceg.osu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-06/Coifman_and_Li_2017.pdf) document huge acceleration noise; Montanino & Punzo published a reconstructed I-80 dataset (TRR 2013, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3141/2390-11). Two takeaways: (i) calibrate against reconstructed NGSIM or highD, not raw NGSIM; (ii) an acceleration-distribution plausibility check is itself a realism benchmark for a simulator's output.

4) Aggregate/flow-level realism: fundamental diagram (flow-density-speed) from virtual loop detectors compared to real FD scatter: reproduce lane capacity (~1800-2400 veh/h/ln), queue-discharge capacity drop (~5-15%, Cassidy & Bertini 1999), congested wave speed (~15-20 km/h). Headway realism: KS/AD tests on time-headway distributions vs loop event data (classic: 'Examining Headway Distribution Models with Urban Freeway Loop Event Data'; recent SUMO example using KS on saturation headways: https://doi.org/10.3390/su18147025). Queue lengths and degree-of-saturation at signals as calibration targets: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590198220301421. Platoon dispersion vs Robertson's model (TRANSYT) closes the signal-corridor gap.

5) Modern distributional/scenario-level realism: Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC) meta-metric — NLL of real logged trajectories under the simulator's induced distribution across kinematic, interactive, map-based components, 32 rollouts/scenario (https://ml4ad.github.io/files/papers2023/The%20Waymo%20Open%20Sim%20Agents%20Challenge.pdf; overview https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/waymo-open-sim-agents-challenge-wosac). 2024-2026 imitation-learning traffic sim papers evaluate exactly this way. A 2024/2025 pNEUMA-based SUMO calibration study reports the final configuration reduced Wasserstein distance by ~55.8% vs default SUMO (found via https://zenodo.org/records/10491409 / pNEUMA literature) — i.e., Wasserstein-distance-on-feature-distributions is a workable iterate-and-benchmark objective.

== B. V2X COMMUNICATION: metrics, campaigns, numbers ==

1) PDR-vs-distance vs named campaigns. GM campaigns (Bai, Stancil, Krishnan, MobiCom 2010, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/1859995.1860033) — the classic DSRC empirical PDR characterization from realistic driving (freeway/rural/urban), showing distance-dependent PDR decay with a wide stochastic gray zone; companion GM work defines effective range (PDR above threshold) vs maximum range. Safety Pilot Model Deployment empirical study (arXiv:1606.08365, https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08365) — world's largest CV test (~2,800 equipped vehicles, Ann Arbor); quantifies max/effective DSRC range and degradation from trees, buildings, weather, elevation; the underlying BSM logs are public (ITS DataHub, data.transportation.gov) and directly usable as reference distributions for BSM timing and GPS/speed noise. Urban V2I benchmark (Sensors 2021, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8347901/): 802.11p LoS good PDR to ~700 m; NLoS urban dramatically shorter. DLR field test (de Ponte Müller et al., ITS World Congress 2021, https://elib.dlr.de/142341/1/ITS-G5_and_C-V2X_Link_Level_Performance_Measurements_dePonteMueller_v4.0.pdf — numbers extracted from PDF): Cohda MK5 (ITS-G5) vs MK6c (C-V2X) vehicle-to-RSU; ITS-G5 min E2E latency 5 ms @200 B -> 8-9 ms @800/1000 B; C-V2X E2E ~25 ms -> 40-45 ms (1-sigma) @800/1000 B (SPS-dominated); C-V2X PER ~0% -> 10-13% (1-sigma) for 800/1000 B and earlier NLoS connectivity loss than ITS-G5; also cross-channel interference results (C-V2X PER 0% -> 5% when ITS-G5 moved into channel 184). C-V2X Mode 4 experimental validation of PC5 exists (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/364166252) and Anritsu lab latency methodology (https://www.automotivetestingtechnologyinternational.com/features/latency-performance-testing-the-lte-v2x-pc5-interface.html). Simulation-side C-V2X anchor: PDR 95% at 380/300/280 m for 0.1/0.2/0.3 veh/m at MCS 9 (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-21967-2_45); open ns-3 C-V2X mode 4 model of Eckermann et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.09977, code https://github.com/FabianEckermann/ns-3_c-v2x).

2) Channel load / CBR: ETSI DCC (TS 102 687 / TS 103 175, https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/103100_103199/103175/01.01.01_60/ts_103175v010101p.pdf; survey https://repositori.upf.edu/bitstreams/f22235ad-c5f3-4211-9463-c213c5697bbf/download): satisfactory CBR range 0.55-0.75, control loops hold ~0.6; CBR measured as busy fraction over 1 s probes. A realism benchmark is CBR-vs-density curves: at high density an uncontrolled 10 Hz beaconing fleet must push CBR toward/past these levels and PDR must degrade accordingly (channel congestion coupling). 3GPP C-V2X analog: CBR from S-RSSI with CR limits per priority.

3) Awareness metrics: neighbor-awareness ratio (detected/present neighbors within nominal range + position freshness) — EURECOM 'Rethinking Cooperative Awareness for Future V2X Safety-critical Applications' (https://www.eurecom.fr/publication/5365/download/comsys-publi-5365.pdf); minimum Awareness Failure Distance (mAFD) (https://doi.org/10.3390/s24186086). These are the application-level counterpart of PDR and are what misbehavior detectors actually experience.

4) Validated propagation models to copy: Sommer's empirical 802.11p obstacle-shadowing model (WONS 2011, https://www.david-eckhoff.net/pdf/sommer2011computationally.pdf) — per-building attenuation calibrated against city measurements, 'very high accuracy' at marginal cost; Veins ships it plus two-ray interference (https://veins.car2x.org/); GEMV^2 (Boban et al.) is the other measurement-validated geometry-based V2V packet-level model. These give a cheap path to defensible LoS/NLoS behavior in a custom Python radio model: distance path-loss + per-obstacle-count attenuation + stochastic fading term.

== C. VeReMi family: how validated, how criticized ==

Original VeReMi (van der Heijden et al., SecureComm 2018; https://veremi-dataset.github.io/): VEINS/OMNeT++/SUMO on the LuST Luxembourg subscenario; 225 simulations = 5 position-attack types x 3 traffic densities x 3 attacker fractions x 5 seeds. Documented critiques: (i) no physical sensor/GPS error model — benign positions were exact, so position falsification is trivially separable (this is the headline fix motivating VeReMi Extension — Kamel et al., 'VeReMi Extension', ICC 2020, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/340547411; adds realistic sensor error models, 19 attack types incl. speed/timing/replay/DoS/Sybil, two densities, generated with the F2MD framework); (ii) limited attack diversity and naive constant-offset implementations; (iii) simplistic physical layer — motivated physical-layer plausibility work (So et al., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333184222); (iv) no train/val/test splits -> incomparable, leakage-prone ML evaluations; (v) aging LuST scenario and 802.11p-only stack. VeReMi NextGen (Ulm 2026, https://oparu.uni-ulm.de/items/a1a874b1-c15a-4f8d-9fae-082368353aaf; overview https://veremi-dataset.github.io/) responds: Eclipse MOSAIC + SUMO + OMNeT++ on InTAS (Ingolstadt), urban+highway, low/high density, 3 driver profiles (normal/cautious/aggressive), 15 curated attacks over position/speed/acceleration/heading/timing, predefined ML splits, public generator, CC-BY on Zenodo. Residual critiques that still apply to ALL VeReMi generations (echoed in 2024-2025 ML-MBD papers, e.g. VeMisNet https://doi.org/10.3390/jsan14050100): simulation-reality gap (no real RF interference/power heterogeneity), single-scenario external validity, near-saturated accuracies suggesting shortcut learning on simulator artifacts. For an SCMS/MA dataset project the actionable checklist is: sensor-error models on benign traffic, attack diversity with randomized parameters, held-out scenario/domain splits, and a published generator + datasheet.

== D. Public reference data for calibration ==

Trajectories (car-following/lane-change): NGSIM I-80 & US-101 (FHWA, 10 Hz, free; use Montanino-Punzo reconstructed I-80, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3141/2390-11); highD (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/329611995 — German highways, drone, 25 Hz, ~110,000 vehicles, ~44,500 driven km, position error typically <10 cm; academic license) + siblings inD/rounD/exiD for intersections/roundabouts/merges; pNEUMA (Athens CBD, 10 drones, 5 days, 1.3 km^2, ~100 km-lanes, ~100 intersections, ~500,000 trajectories; open on Zenodo https://zenodo.org/records/10491409; paper https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0968090X19310320); pNEUMA Vision extension (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0968090X22003795). Loop detectors / counts: UTD19 (ETH Zurich, https://utd19.ethz.ch/ — 23,541 stationary detectors, 40 cities, 3-5 min aggregation; largest open multi-city set; refined subset B22: 10,150 detectors, 25 cities); Caltrans PeMS (tens of thousands of freeway detectors, 30 s/5 min, free registration) — both give real flow/occupancy/speed and empirical FDs and headway statistics per city type. OD/demand + ready SUMO scenarios: LuST (Luxembourg 24 h), TAPASCologne (~700k trips/24 h), MoST Monaco, InTAS Ingolstadt (already used by this project and by VeReMi NextGen — InTAS itself was calibrated against real Ingolstadt counts, so its published demand is a legitimate reference). V2X field data: Safety Pilot Model Deployment BSM database (public sample via USDOT ITS DataHub) for real BSM inter-arrival times, GPS error, and DSRC reception statistics.
recommendations: Build an automated per-run 'realism scorecard' (JSON emitted by every simulation run, tracked in CI/regression tests) with two panels. Traffic panel: GEH pass-rate over virtual detectors (gates: GEH<5 for >=85% of detectors, GEH<4 on total flow, total volume within 5%), KS statistic + Wasserstein distance on time-headway/speed/acceleration distributions vs a pinned reference (highD-derived for highway scenarios, pNEUMA/UTD19-derived for urban), and fundamental-diagram parameters (capacity 1800-2400 veh/h/ln, capacity drop 5-15%, wave speed 15-20 km/h). Comm panel: PDR-vs-distance curve (binned, with RMSE vs a pinned published reference curve), latency percentiles (p50/p95), CBR vs density, neighbor-awareness ratio at 100/200/300 m. This directly implements 'benchmark at every step then continue iterating'.

Validate the built-in IDM car-following against highD using the Kurtc/Punzo protocol: per-pair calibration minimizing spacing RMSPE, report calibration and holdout validation error; accept if calibration RMSPE is in the 5-15% band and validation in the 15-30% band (below the inter-driver variability floor is overfitting, above ~30% is a modeling problem). Add a hard physical-plausibility gate: simulated accelerations within roughly -8..+4 m/s^2 with a realistic distribution (the NGSIM critique in reverse).

Adopt the FHWA 2019 distribution-based criteria for scenario-level gates rather than single-number matching: run >=10 seeds per scenario to build the simulated distribution, and check 95%-within-2-sigma / 66%-within-1-sigma of a multi-day (or multi-seed reference) envelope for detector counts and route travel times. For the InTAS urban scenario, use InTAS's published calibrated demand as the field reference; for generic urban distributions use UTD19 city detectors.

Calibrate the 'range-limited lossy radio' against published PDR-vs-distance shapes instead of a hard range cutoff: three-regime curve (reliable zone / stochastic gray zone / cutoff), LoS parameters anchored to 802.11p field data (high PDR to ~500-700 m at 20 dBm) and NLoS via a Sommer-style per-obstacle attenuation term (11 dB first wall + per-meter term, WONS 2011 values) — cheap to implement in pure Python and measurement-validated. Benchmark latency against DLR numbers (802.11p: 5-9 ms; C-V2X: 25-45 ms) depending on which stack the scenario claims to model.

Add channel-load realism if attack/detection results depend on density: compute CBR from the message schedule and verify high-density scenarios drive CBR toward the ETSI 0.55-0.75 range with corresponding PDR degradation; if the radio model cannot produce this coupling, document it as a known unrealism (it changes misbehavior-report loss patterns at rush hour).

Calibrate benign-message noise against the public Safety Pilot Model Deployment BSM data (real GPS position/speed error and BSM inter-arrival jitter). This addresses the single most-cited realism critique of VeReMi-style datasets (error-free benign kinematics making attacks linearly separable) and materially affects detector ROC curves in the MA dataset.

Inherit the VeReMi-critique checklist for dataset credibility (the project's DATASHEET.md is the right vehicle): document sensor-error models, attack parameter randomization ranges, per-family train/val/test splits with scenario/domain holdout (not random-row splits), and seeds/manifests for byte-reproducibility — plus an explicit 'known unrealisms' section (simulation-reality gap, single-stack radio).

Optional, higher effort: adopt a WOSAC-style scalar realism meta-metric (NLL of held-out real trajectory features under simulated rollout distributions across kinematic/interactive components) as the single tracked number when iterating on traffic behavior; for comparing full simulators, use MOSAIC's OMNeT++/ns-3 federate (WSL) or ms-van3t as a high-fidelity comm oracle to spot-check the Python radio model's PDR/CBR/latency curves on identical mobility traces.

tools.name: SUMO calibration tooling (calibrators, routeSampler.py, E1/E2 detector outputs, TraCI)
tools.what: Turn real counts into demand (routeSampler), place virtual induction loops matching real detector layouts, and enforce flow/speed at edges (calibrator objects); the natural way to produce GEH-comparable outputs from the MOSAIC/SUMO path already in this project.

tools.name: scipy/statsmodels (KS, Anderson-Darling, Wasserstein) + ~30 lines of GEH code
tools.what: Implements the entire statistical layer of the realism scorecard: GEH per detector, KS/AD tests on headway/speed/accel distributions, Wasserstein distance on feature distributions.
tools.windows_feasibility: Trivial (pure Python, already in the project's toolchain)
tools.integration_effort: Low — a scms_sim_ref 'realism' module + pytest regression gates

tools.name: highD / inD / rounD / exiD datasets + published Python readers
tools.what: Drone trajectory data (25 Hz, <10 cm error) for car-following and lane-change calibration/validation of the built-in IDM simulator; highD for highway scenarios, inD for signalized/unsignalized urban junctions.
tools.integration_effort: Low-medium — free academic license request, then a calibration script (per-pair spacing-RMSPE)

tools.name: pNEUMA (Zenodo) and UTD19 (ETH) open datasets
tools.what: pNEUMA: ~500k urban trajectories (Athens) for urban car-following/queue/headway references; UTD19: 23,541 loop detectors in 40 cities for real flow-occupancy fundamental diagrams and count distributions to benchmark urban scenarios distributionally.
tools.integration_effort: Low — reference-distribution extraction scripts, pinned as scorecard baselines

tools.name: Montanino-Punzo reconstructed NGSIM I-80 (+ raw NGSIM US-101)
tools.what: Cleaned classic trajectory data for car-following calibration cross-checks; also the source of the acceleration-plausibility realism gate.

tools.name: Safety Pilot Model Deployment BSM data (USDOT ITS DataHub)
tools.what: Real DSRC BSM logs (~2,800 vehicles, Ann Arbor): GPS/speed noise distributions, BSM inter-arrival jitter, and reception statistics — the field reference for making benign V2X messages non-ideal (the core VeReMi realism fix).
tools.integration_effort: Medium — fit noise/jitter models, wire into the BSM/CAM generator

tools.name: Veins (OMNeT++) validated radio models: Sommer obstacle shadowing + two-ray interference; GEMV^2
tools.what: Measurement-validated 802.11p propagation models; use either as a coupled high-fidelity oracle or (cheaper) port their published closed-form attenuation equations into the project's Python radio model.
tools.maturity: Mature, the standard in VANET research; VeReMi lineage uses it
tools.windows_feasibility: Veins/OMNeT++ runs on Windows; porting the equations needs nothing
tools.integration_effort: Low to port the equations; high to fully couple Veins

tools.name: Eclipse MOSAIC network-simulator federates (SNS / OMNeT++ / ns-3) and ms-van3t (ns-3 V2X framework)
tools.what: MOSAIC (already in the toolchain) can swap its simple network simulator for OMNeT++/ns-3 federates to generate reference PDR/CBR/latency curves on identical mobility traces; ms-van3t adds 802.11p + LTE-V2X + NR-V2X stacks with SUMO coupling, actively maintained 2024-2026.
tools.maturity: MOSAIC federation mature; ms-van3t active research-grade
tools.windows_feasibility: MOSAIC core runs on Windows; the OMNeT++/ns-3 federates and ms-van3t effectively require Linux/WSL
tools.integration_effort: High — reserve for periodic spot-check benchmarks, not every iteration

tools.name: F2MD (Framework for Misbehavior Detection, Kamel et al.) + VeReMi NextGen generator
tools.what: The generators behind VeReMi Extension/NextGen: reference implementations of sensor error models, attack catalogs, and label pipelines — the project's third_party/veremi-nextgen submodule makes NextGen the natural comparability baseline for the MA dataset.
tools.maturity: Research-grade but the de-facto standard in this niche
tools.windows_feasibility: NextGen uses MOSAIC/SUMO/OMNeT++ (partially WSL); reading its configs/models needs nothing
tools.integration_effort: Medium — mirror its sensor-error and split conventions rather than run it wholesale

tools.name: waymo-open-dataset WOSAC metrics package
tools.what: Reference implementation of the distributional realism meta-metric (NLL over kinematic/interactive/map components) if a single scalar trajectory-realism score is wanted.
tools.windows_feasibility: pip package is Linux-only — needs WSL; or reimplement the simple NLL histogram version in numpy
